title: Autism vs ADHD: 5 Key Differences Explained

segments.text: Is it autism,
or is it ADHD?
It's easy to get these two confused.
Today we're breaking down 5 key differences
between ASD and ADHD,
because although these two might sound similar,
they're definitely not the same.
A lot of autistic folks also have ADHD,
but that's a different video that I'll link below.
You should watch that one next,
but for now, let's talk  about the real differences,
starting with
Number 1
Processing Time
Thinking Slow versus Fast.
If you're autistic, you'll often  need time to process things.
Someone says something,
and your brain takes a minute to think about it.
Or five.
Or a year.
It's like your thoughts are on delay.
Sometimes by the time you're ready to respond,
the conversation has probably moved on,
and you're left scrambling to catch up
or just off in your own conversation
about that thing three topics ago
that you wanted to say something about.
I don't even know what people  are talking about half the time.
I don't even know what I'm  talking about half the time.
With ADHD, thoughts are coming at you fast.
Your brain is firing off ideas
quicker than you can keep up,
and you might interrupt or blurt things out
just to get them out before they're gone.
But your brain doesn't stop with one thought
no-no-no
it keeps going, taking you off
on all kinds of other directions too.
I've seen this with kids I've taught.
Many of the neurodivergent students
have these incredible ideas,
but they really struggle with when to share them.
During class discussions,
you can really see this contrast.
The students with ADHD are  often jumping in rapid fire
Bam-Bam-Bam-Bam-Bam
even when they're trying so hard not to interrupt,
but the thoughts are just begging to come out,
and so, come out they do.
The autistic students often need
more time and space to think,
so putting them on the spot
isn't comfortable for them at all.
But sometimes later in the lesson,
or the next day, or even the next week,
that's when they're ready to talk about
whatever it was, and when they're ready to talk,
you better be ready to listen.
Let me tell you.
ASD takes its time,
and sometimes you might only realize
what was happening hours,  days, or even weeks later.
Oh, that's what they meant!
ADHD is often running ahead,  jumping to another spot
before sometimes being  pulled back by other people.
And even though both brains ruminate,
the reasons for this are often different.
With the autistic brain, connecting things later,
and the ADHD brain, often  second guessing what happened
because of something I'll talk about right now.
Impulsivity versus Slow Build
ADHD brains often make snap decisions.
They're impulsive, whether  it's buying something random
and sometimes really freaking expensive,
or saying whatever pops into  your head as it appears,
or acting on the exact feeling  you're having in the moment,
even if that means saying something
you might regret later.
Your brain doesn't wait for you to process,
it says,
"Let's go!"
and you're off,
but if you're autistic, there's  usually more of a slow build.
Your emotions or stress build  up quietly in the background
until it gets too much,
then,
Boom!
out comes the meltdown or shutdown.
At least that's how it can look to an observer.
As an autistic person, I  might feel the build inside,
but not really know what to do with it either,
so that's why in point number 1
I said both brains ruminate.
ADHD brains are often replaying things,
worried about what they said or did,
and whether it was okay.
Autistic brains might be putting things together
long after, which is why the rumination happens.
The "oh, that's what they meant"
might come hours, days, or even weeks later.
I mean, there was a time in elementary school
that I got in trouble, and  I didn't even realize why
until I was an adult and diagnosed with autism.
The memories of getting in trouble
for saying something honest
that was looked at as mean.
But really,
how could it be mean to tell a girl
that her drawing was really cool
because it looked like a combination
of a dragon and a chicken,
and a little bit like a dinosaur.
How was I supposed to know
that she wanted to draw a horse,
and that she was going to cry a bunch after.
The swift reaction of the teacher
and the forced apology I had to utter
when I didn't even know  what I was apologizing for,
all of that still popped up in my brain,
so many years later.
All I learned at the time was  that I got in trouble a lot,
but now science knows that impulsivity is common
for ADHDers,
and longer processing times
are common for autistic people.
So to sum it up,
ADHD is often quick and impulsive,
and ASD is usually a slow buildup.
Number 3
Routines versus Spontaneity.
Routines feel safe and  soothing when you're autistic.
Knowing exactly what to expect
brings a sense of calm and control.
Any disruption to that routine,
well it kind of feels like  your world got totally rocked,
thrown around, and flipped upside down,
and you landed on your head,
and then somebody stepped on your kidney,
when all you wanted to do
was watch a nature show on sharks.
What was I talking about again?
So autistic brains want to keep repetition,
and routines are exactly that,
which is why travel or even taking time off work
can be hard for an autistic person.
It's not that we don't need a break.
We often really do.
It's just that we really  like a consistent schedule.
For me, I like it so much that even on weekends
I still work pretty consistently.
I also go to bed and wake up around the same time,
whether it's a weekend, or  a holiday, or a workday.
Those routines help my brain feel comfortable,
because I know what's happening.
I also like my work, so that helps too,
and I also like sharks,
which has absolutely nothing  to do with this video,
but still probably important.
What was I talking about again?
Now for ADHD folks, routines can feel stifling.
You thrive on unpredictability.
If things get too predictable,
your brain starts to get a little bit mischievous
and looks for something new.
Anything to break the monotony.
Why?
An ADHD brain gets little rushes of dopamine
from novelty,
so that's why an ADHD might do something
impulsive and spontaneous
before fully thinking it through.
And it's why routines can feel boring,
monotonous, and completely unnecessary
to an ADHD brain.
It'll actively resist it.
The pull from both sides
is where it gets a little bit tricky
for autistic brains that also have ADHD.
And by tricky I mean insane.
We talk about that lots in other videos,
so if you think you have both,
check out the videos in the description.
So to sum things up,
autistic brains love routines for stability,
while ADHD brains crave a bit of chaos
to have more novelty in life,
which for me, usually leads
to diarrhea.
Number 4
Focus: Monotropic versus Multitasking
If you're autistic, your focus is intense.
When you're on something,  you're all in, no distractions.
But the problem is, once you're interrupted,
it's hard to get back into that zone,
which is why you might appear  to get irrationally irritated
when you get interrupted by someone else,
or by your stomach growling,
or by the urge to go to the bathroom,
or by the fact that you might actually
have to go to sleep in the next 72 hours.
Your brain is often in a tunnel vision state.
You don't hear things
and you don't perceive time.
If a herd of bison stampeded  through your living room,
you wouldn't hear it.
Why?
Because you're in it, and by in it,
I mean in it to win it,
and you'll really want to  chug through until the end
because autistic inertia and  your your monotropic brain
are pulling you there.
Pause to do something else?
No thank you!
Time for a meeting?
No, can't you see I'm busy?
Responding to you when you ask me if I'm busy?
Feeling a little
shy
With ADHD, multitasking is the norm:
music playing,
having a conversation while you're typing an email
and you're also feeding your pet goldfish
at the same time,
but, wait, while you got out the goldfish food
that reminded you of buying cat food.
Now you're searching Amazon for cat food,
but you see that wish list item:
your new speakers.
They're on sale.
-Wait. You were listening to music,
and also talking,
-is that person still on the line?
Oopsies!
If you have ADHD, your  brain is constantly bouncing
between 10 things at once,
but the catch?
None of them ever get finished.
Your brain is busy jumping around everywhere,
trying to finish one task.
It's like your brain is  interrupting you constantly
and pulling you off in all  these different directions,
but it's not your fault.
It's part of having ADHD.
Your focus is the opposite of an autistic person
doing just one thing,
like having a conversation,
seems like wasting time
when you could be doing  five things simultaneously.
Both ADHDers and autistic people
often struggle with interruptions,
but autistic people are often stuck In the zone,
and and ADHD brains can't stay on one thing
long enough to finish it.
But both can hyper-focus,
it just takes a different  environment for each brain.
Number 5
Planners versus Procrastinators
Autistic people can zone in with laser focus,
and once your autistic brain  is in the right environment,
it takes a mind-shattering earthquake
to break your concentration.
But when that focus is interrupted,
getting back into the groove  can feel nearly impossible,
and you'll probably want to grab
the nearest breakable item
and hurl it across the room.
This can make it stressful  when your focus gets broken
by a looming deadline.
That's why a lot of autistic  people try to do things early.
They want to get it done in  a predictable, planned way.
It's very soothing to autistic brains,
even if it can be hard to plan
due to executive functioning challenges at times.
ADHD folks are constantly juggling
the focus of their attention.
Your attention is split between  too many things at once,
which means it's hard to focus on one task,
except when you do get honed in on something,
or when a deadline is looming.
It's like you're in another world,
and everything else fades out.
ADHDers are often master procrastinators.
It might also take some outside pressure
and the threat of a deadline,
but clarity happens,
and suddenly that thing gets done,
fast.
Someone I knew in college was like this.
She would just delay things and put them off,
but then one or two nights before it was due,
she'd just sit for hours and  hours and get it all finished.
She'd still get really good grades,
but it was like she couldn't think
or force herself to do it
without the deadline approaching.
She'd say the pressure helped her focus,
whereas for me, just watching her study habits
gave me anxiety and diarrhea.
How could she possibly prefer
to wait to do things to the end?
What if she didn't finish?
How could she not want to  plan things step by step?
I got an assignment and started working on it,
usually that day.
Pace it out.
Make sure I had plenty of time to get it done.
She did the complete opposite,
so it was a good example
of how differently our brains worked.
So both types of brains  can experience hyper-focus,
but the autistic brains need
a special and particular environment to get there,
where ADHD brains just sometimes
fall into it by circumstance.
So again, wondering how these might look together
in the same brain?
You'll have to watch this next  video to hear all about it,
and the chaos of the two in one brain
can get pretty insane,
let me tell you.
Trust me, I know.
